Hey kiddo, Handsome Jack here... Again. So apparently you want me to review Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. Yeah, my game. Well, technically it isn't my game, because some people down in Australia made it, but let's not get distracted by geography. First of all, this game is fantastic because it finally gives you the most important thing Borderlands was missing: more me. You get to see how I became the handsome, brilliant, completely misunderstood hero you all know and love. And before you start with the whole "Jack is the villain" thing, just stop. You weren't there. You didn't see what I saw. You didn't have to deal with Roland, Lilith, Vault Hunters, idiots, moon rocks, or Australians. I did. And frankly, I handled it pretty well. The Pre-Sequel takes you to the moon, gives you low gravity, butt slams, laser guns, cryo weapons, and oxygen tanks, which means you can jump higher, freeze people, and then slam into them from orbit. That's science, kiddo. That's progress. The low-gravity movement is actually fantastic, too. You bounce around the battlefield like some kind of heavily armed kangaroo, which is exactly what the future of warfare should look like. And the guns? Great. The lasers are great. The cryo weapons are great. The moon is great. Everything is great. Except Claptrap. Claptrap is not great. Claptrap is a crime against software engineering.

And the characters? Oh, they're fantastic. You get Athena, Nisha, Wilhelm, Aurelia, Claptrap, ugh, and they each have their own abilities and playstyles. Wilhelm starts off as a normal guy and, well... let's just say things get a little Hyperion-y for him. Nisha is basically "What if shooting people was a personality?" Aurelia is a rich ice queen who makes being unpleasant look like an Olympic sport. And Claptrap is there because apparently someone in the development team had a personal vendetta against me. But here's the important part: you get to watch me become me. You see the idealistic version of Jack, the guy who genuinely thinks he's saving everyone. You see him make decisions that seem reasonable at first. Then another decision. Then another. And eventually you're sitting there going, "Ohhhhhh. That's why he becomes the guy from Borderlands 2." Exactly. That's called character development, kiddo. You're welcome. And yes, the game is funny. It's ridiculous. It's got Australians yelling at you, robots exploding, people dying, moon physics, and enough fourth-wall-breaking nonsense to make you wonder if the developers forgot you were playing a game. Don't worry, I didn't. I know you're there. I know you're sitting in front of that screen. I know you're listening to me talk. And I know you're probably skipping half of these dialogue scenes because you think you have somewhere better to be. You don't. You have Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. This is your life now.

Now, is it better than Borderlands 2? Well... no. Let's not get crazy. Borderlands 2 is better paced, has a bigger world, and, most importantly, has me being absolutely incredible in it. The Pre-Sequel can get repetitive, the moon can feel a little empty, and there are moments where you're running around collecting oxygen like a depressed astronaut with a gun. But you know what? I don't care. Because this game does something incredibly important: it makes you understand me. And that's something Borderlands 2 never really lets you do. You don't just fight Jack here. You watch him fall. You watch him become obsessed. You watch him lose his grip on reality while everyone around him keeps telling him he's wrong. And maybe, just maybe, you start thinking, "Hey... Jack wasn't completely crazy." See? That's the trick. That's how I get you. By the end, you're not just playing a prequel. You're watching the birth of the most handsome, talented, brilliant, and tragically underappreciated man in the history of Pandora. So I'm giving The Pre-Sequel a 9 out of 10. I'd give it a 10, but I'm saving that extra point for myself. Also, the game has a 9 out of 10 because I said so. I actually just changed the review score in the game files. You're welcome. And if you disagree, that's fine. I'm not mad. I'm just going to quietly add your name to a list. It's nothing. Probably.

At release, you will find many bugs, some game-breaking. The ones talked about most are quest items flying into unreachable areas, or NPCs getting stuck in walls causing a restart. These of course will be fixed, but right now be aware they are present.

The Low-Gravity and Oxygen aspects are a nice experiment, but let me tell you the sheer amount of oxygen thrown at you when you dont need it, and the lack when you do, makes it such a god damn chore, you wonder why its even in the game. Oh and BTW you are the only one with a limit on your oxygen, the enemies and NPCs can wander around infinitely without having to replenish theirs. So while you're scrambling to find that O2 they're floating towards you following you whereever you go. Oh and pretty much every enemy has a jetpack and always follows so theres no more hiding and using cover.

The Low Gravity makes traveling the world quicker, and engaging enemies faster, which is counter balanced by fighting off enemies by the hundreds. The firefights get so tedious and boring you'll find yourself frequently hitting ESC to take a break. Forget about using the Low Gravity to reach neat and cool areas, because theres nothing to find, no hidden chests like in the older titles, what you will find however, are invisible walls, random spots that instant kill you, getting stuck somewhere you cant jump out and even falling through the world. 

The Butt-Slam is also a nice little experiment but in actuality, it does more harm than good. You deal more damage shooting enemies in mid air for some reason, and can manuever more easily gliding around in the low gravity. The Second you Butt-Slam down to deal minimal damage to your enemies, this makes you a prime target from all the melee and jet-pack 'Scavs' and you'll find yourself fighting for your life frequently after butt-slamming.

Just about every quest is some kind of Fetch-Quest and will drive you across the world to flip a switch, then have to cross to the other side to flip another, with many boring and slow fire-fights between. Sometimes you'll flip a switch only to find that for some reason it didnt work, and to resolve it, is to go somewhere else and flip another, but wait that didnt work either, well guess what theres one more switch back at the other side of the world you can flip that may get it going. You'll enter an enemy stronghold only to find they locked the door, forcing you to crawl your way through what is now  a maze of a base to unlock that door, return, and enter it. Once inside, guess what, another locked door causing you to crawl through.

The bosses, are boring, and forgettable. Really all you have to do is shoot them from a far and avoid their attacks. They dont have much life to them either, some even lack animations. They're like a floating statue that talks and shoots at you, they dont even move. Atleast with borderlands 2, the opening scenes were very interesting and well designed. Boom Bewm, Bad Maw, the Bunker, Flynt. They were all interesting, unique and had amazing opening scenes. In TPS, every boss is like fighting Wilhelm in BL2. I've played a lot of game sequels that have been panned by their fans in my time as a PC gamer. [i]Mass Effect: Andromeda[/i], [i]Dead Space 3[/i], and [i]BioShock: Infinite[/i] are all games that I would describe as being heavily flawed, but still possessing a solid foundation in one way or another. I wouldn't ever lump this game in with the others though, as I consider it to be one of the most underappreciated sequels in gaming. 

Developed by the now-defunct 2K Australia, and set in-between the first and second Borderlands titles, [i]Borderlands: The Pre-sequel[/i] has you take on the role of one of four vault hunters hired by Hyperion to find a vault on Pandora's moon, Elpis. However, rather than focus on the hunt for the vault, the vast bulk of the game is spent chronicling the descent of a man named Jack into the villain known as Handsome Jack. You see him go from an affable antihero to a despot who will stop at nothing to take his revenge on those who slight him. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]

 - Possibly the best set of playable characters in the series, with a diverse set of abilities, and what I consider to be the best character progression system in the series. 

 - Weapons feel far more diverse than BL2, although it still doesn't feel nearly as fleshed out as BL1s guns. Two new additions to the weapon generation system- the laser weapon type and the cryo elemental type- are fantastic additions that greatly enhance the player experience. 

 - The low-gravity movement and oxygen system is a fantastic addition that feels great to play around with, and gives players much more mobility through the game world. 

 - Other great gameplay features include the Grinder (which allows you to take old weapons and create newer and better weapons, meaning that even white-rarity weapons have a use now), bounce pads, and much faster access to character abilities than BL1 and BL2. 

 - Excellent character writing, including fully voiced player characters, a series first. 

 - Level design, while slightly less open than the second game, is well-done, with a wide variety of locations. 

 - The art style has also changed from the post-apocalyptic setting of Pandora to a more space-age look befitting Elpis. 

 - Music is also less western-inspired, and has a much greater focus on electronic instruments and synth-music. 

[h1]CONS:[/h1]

 - As a player character, Claptrap suffers from a very random special ability that often makes him a liability in multiplayer and singleplayer alike. The fact that the series' pet punching bag is also the fourth playable character is also quite annoying, as you will have to endure his frakking voice for twenty hours of the campaign if you pick him as your vault hunter. 

 - Boss fights are both rarer than in BL2, and suffer from reduced quality, smaller loot tables, and were initially not replayable outside of a UVHM New Game + run. Indeed, Zarpadon still cannot be fought a second time to get any unique loot you missed, meaning her boss fight feels less rewarding from a extrinsically motivated perspective. 
 
 - The balancing in this game is extremely poor. I completed almost every side quest I came across, and still ran into beefy enemies who downed me very quickly in the end game. Even in the early game, you will often run into enemies who down you very quickly regardless of whether you've been grinding out levels and loot the entire time. 

 - While the story is fantastically written, it is one of the worst paced stories I've ever experienced, with a endgame that drags on for far too long, and suffers from extreme checkpoint starvation. Sidequests also dry up around the time you finish the Helios section of the game, so good luck getting more levels without endlessly grinding enemies in the world! 

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]

Overall, I would say that fans are often way too harsh on this game, considering how much it experiments with the Borderlands formula. [i]Borderlands 3[/i], while I haven't played it yet, seems to be far weaker than this game, with the main antagonists being bloody [i]Twitch Streamers[/i] for crying out loud. While this game suffers from problems that could have been remedied with more resources and more post-launch content, it is far better as a story, and has far greater potential as a elevator pitch. 8.5/10, recommended.

Quick Summary – Did you enjoy Borderlands 1 and Borderlands 2 for their gunplay, loot farming, irreverent humor, and cooperative gameplay? Then you should enjoy the Pre-Sequel as well. The story may not be as compelling, but it does fill in some gaps from the previous games and brings back one of the greatest characters in all of video gaming: Handsome Jack (but less crazy). 

The reason the game is called the “pre-sequel” is because the story is being narrated after the end of Borderlands 2, however you’re playing the story as it is being told, so the gameplay is actually taking place between the end of the Borderlands 1 DLC and the start of Borderlands 2. You play as one of 4 Vault Hunters (6 if you own the Season Pass) trying to help a mid-level Hyperion Corporation employee (Jack) who is defending a space station against a horde of soldiers from a rival corporation. If you’ve played part 1 and 2, you will recognize all 4 of the “new” vault hunters. Your battles will range from the mostly empty Hyperion space station to the surface of Pandora’s moon: Elpis. The previous Borderlands games took place on the planet Pandora, and you will notice that Elpis has much lower gravity and no air, along with much less wildlife. Your ultimate goal in the game is not only expelling the mysterious soldiers laying siege to the Helios space station, but also finding the fabled alien Vault on the moon’s surface and claiming all the awesome loot inside. 

Just like the previous Borderlands games, the Pre-Sequel is played in First Person Shooter perspective with a massive variety of guns, grenades, personal shield mods, and “class mods” which give bonuses to specific character classes. Each character class has 3 “skill trees” to allow you to customize your hero with abilities as you level up. If you haven’t played any Borderlands games before, the level progression system here is kind of similar to the Dead Island game series, where you get 1 skill point every time you level up and choose where to put it. Note that just like the previous Borderlands games, you can “re-spec” your skills very easily, so feel free to experiment with skills to see what you like best. 

You should get Borderlands the Pre-Sequel if:
+You liked the gameplay of Borderlands 1 and 2. With only a few additions such as low gravity areas, laser guns, and oxygen kits, you will be right at home here. Core gameplay is practically identical to the previous games. I mentioned earlier that there is less wildlife on Elpis, and this means that the vast majority of enemies in the Pre-Sequel are human solders… with guns. Melee combat is less effective in this game because human enemies like to back away from you if you try charging at them.
+You like the story aspect of the Borderlands games, and want to know more about the characters from previous games. The people on Elpis mostly speak with Australian accents, and honestly I’m not sure if they’re purposely speaking gibberish a lot of time. There is a lot of background story on characters from the previous game that you may enjoy, along with the Borderlands humor that you have come to expect.
+The best part of all three Borderlands games is the ability to play the campaign co-operatively with friends or internet strangers. People can drop into your game and play with you at any time. You don’t need to create a “multiplayer lobby” and wait for someone to join you. It’s much more fun to play the game with companions, especially the “True Vault Hunter” mode, where you can restart the game with all your level ups and gear, but much harder enemies. You will have a hard time beating True Vault Hunter without a friend or two to back you up. Note that it’s kind of hard to find people to play with nowadays. Bring a friend with you instead of hoping to find a stranger to play with.

You should Not get Borderlands the Pre-Sequel if:
-You want something radically different (or better) than Borderlands 1 and 2. Other than the new character classes it will feel like the same gameplay with a new story. 
-You get pissed off by annoying non-player characters who talk funny. There are a couple of them in this game and you’ll wish you could smack them.
-The game is still high in price. The Season Pass hasn’t gone below $15 in North America and only includes 1 big story DLC along with the 2 new player classes. I was able to get the base game for less than $3 because I owned all the other Borderlands games, so I got my money’s worth.

It pains me to see all the hate for The Pre-Sequel. It's a good game that's a lot of fun, but people don't like it because it's not as good as Borderlands 2. Truth be told, they're right, but this is no less of a good game.

TL;DR: Yes, I recommend this game, but no, it's not as good as its predecessor while being all too similar and almost anyone else will tell you the same thing. If you're new to Borderlands and are looking for a good game to start with, start with the second one. If you already own the second one, consider TPS. With that said, the remainder of this review will be focused on those who have already played the second one.

There's plenty that I like about TPS, even in comparison to BL2. The new characters are fun and each have more fufilling stories than previous playable characters (as long as you don't count BL1's characters being major parts of BL2's story, but that's besides the point). The characters are all very different from each other and all the characters we've had in the past. Characters like Roland and Axton are very similar, as is Mordecai to Gaige and Brick to Krieg, and although they all played very differently, characters in TPS felt more fresh than those in BL2, albiet guilty of some similarities as well. Overall, I feel that the characters were thought out well in terms of story, personality, design, and functionality. 

The story itself was satisfying, filling the information gap between Borderlands 1 and 2, the Pre-Sequel delivers on the name that it's sold on. It was great to not only learn about the new characters but the old ones as well - Handsome Jack, particularly. Unless I'm missing something, all questions that I had were answered without any plotholes, paradoxes, or anything else to ruin the story. It fits like a glove and I commend Gearbox on letting this new chunk of story slide seeminglessly into place. They may or may not have had TPS's story in mind when making BL2, I might never know, but they've gotten me to believe it anyway.

Being a bit of a grinding game after the first playthrough, TPS made it more enjoyable to play through it the second, third, and fiftieth times by having the characters interract more with what's going on and have entire changes of NPC dialogue based on who you're playing as. This may seem minor, but it's a breath of fresh air for those who have made it through the gauntlet of maxing out past characters. As much as I love Borderlands, the same dialogue becomes daunting after playing through the story so many times and I was pleasantly surprised to see that this has been remedied. 

As far as everything else that is entirely new, the oxygen boost jumps are great and the butt-slams are really fun and change the pace of righting hoardes of enemies. Together, these are two things I actually miss when I play BL2 and something that I hope stays in a smiliar state for Borderlands 3. Cyro is okay - it's a replacement for slag that better suits the story, but it's a downgrade overall for those who relied on slag in BL2. While I liked the idea of ice and felt that BL2 would have been better with it included, I don't like it as a replacement. Admittedly, it makes much more sense to have than slag, both with the environment and story considered, so I'll have to let this slide. Lasers were a decent new addition, but nothing that wowed me. Glitch guns, on the other hand, were really satisying to get and experiment with and I enjoy them a lot more than Seraph and Pearlescent guns. 

I wouldn't argue for a moment that TPS is better than BL2, but let's be honest, it didn't need to be. BL2 gave everyone what they wanted and TPS is still a good game and an excellent addition to the Borderlands franchise for all of us who wanted more.

First of all, let me start with one thing. This game is surprsingly DARK compared to the last two Borderlands games. Prepare your morality.

Now that that's done, let's carry on.

PROS

+Borderlands The Pre-Sequel does not disappoint. I have to admit, at first I was super worried about dying of oxygen loss, but the devs were able to make it so losing your oxygen doesn't really make you worry. Oxygen is every where, and if you DO run out, your health depleted at around less than 1% per second, so it isn't a threat to you at all.

+The low gravity also helps a lot. The use of buttslams makes it more fun to flank enemies, and makes the combat even more fast-paced. Slams also work in places with oxygen, as long as the area doesn't have aritifcial gravity. This also helps for easy second winds. If you were to jump accross the area, and get shot down, chances are you'll land right close to another bunch of enemies. This gives you an indirect and accidental edge against enemies, which is also good. Additonally, certain oz-kits can make your low-g experience more fun and fluid, I personally use the air control ones.

+Now about lasers, one of the most advertised parts of the game. Let me put this straight, they're awesome, and really powerful. They also act as psuedo-gun types for each brand. You want Dahl Shotguns back? Have A LASER ONE THAT FIRES AROUND 3 LASER BOLTS PER SECOND. There are also different types such as the railguns, beams, and repeaters, but different manufacturers can give each weapon type an edge due to their special attributes.

+Cryo weapons are also fun, and not just in the visual kind of appeal. It's more tactical than slag. Slag was just like "shoot enemies with this and then hit them with this". It even stole corossion's power, which made it even crappier. But cryo is super fun to use. The simple charm of butt stomping a single enemy ( EVEN MORE FUN WITH A TEAM) just puts a smile on my face.

Also, A LOT OF  unique weapons with red text can compete with legendary weapons. Like AN EXPLOSIVE JAKOBS SHOTGUN.

Now we have the CONS. Every game has them.

-Let's start with a really annoying one, the checkpoints aren't kind. The maps are bigger for verticality purposes, but some checkpoints can be too far enough that they end up stingy and unforgiving. 

-Next, the vehicles. While the stingray is a pretty fun vehicle to use, I can't help but feel disappointed in the lack of variety. The moon buggy is okay at best, although it's more of the same with classic Borderlands vehicles.

-Nisha's whip is terrible, unless you get the Law and Order skill tree capstone. Don't expect to melee a lot with her.

-The side missions are the same with past missions, where you have to go and kill the thing while getting the other thing. Personally, I don't mind this since Pre-Sequel has the best combat in a Borderlands game so far, but other people might not.

...Overall, Borderlands TPS is a great time. Unless your emotions will get the better of you SINCE THIS GAME IS PRETTY DARK.

This is not Borderlands 3.  This is a very long Borderlands 2 DLC done by the B-Team.  It feels a bit lazy, but it's still a lot of fun.

The Good: The story is interesting and there's a lot to do. There's four new playable characters and they're gender balanced (the game, as a whole, is excellent in that respect). Low gravity, butt-slams, lasers, freeze attacks and Australian in-jokes round out the new features.

The Bad: There's not really anything bad. There's a few polygon tearing glitches, all minor.

The Lazy: It's the Borderlands 2 engine, so if you were expecting something really new, this isn't it. The writing is not up to Borderlands 2 par. Character gestures are rarely customized resulting in them repeating the same generic ones while talking. There's not nearly the variety of enemies and locations as in Borderlands 2.

The Weird: You can play as Claptrap!  SOLD!  Why wouldn't you want to play as a murderous, incompetant robot?  [Hint: you hate his voice.]  It's about as fun and stupid as you'd imagine.  His action skill is a random version of other Vault Hunter's powers, except done wrong.  Example: You can get two guns like the Gunzerker, but you never stop firing.  It gets a bit confusing when you're talking to other Claptraps.

Compared to most FPS, it's excellent, and this is why I recommend it.  Compared to Borderlands 2, it's not quite up to par, but they set a very high bar.

It's a good game, don't get me wrong. If you liked Borderlands 2, but didn't really reach endgame (IE Max level, UVH OP 8) then you'll like this one just as much. There's not too much difference, save for new mechanics and different characters. But the game hasn't really got any worthwhile endgame content compared to Borderlands 2, so if you like it enough to get through to max level, don't expect to stick around afterwards unless you wanna start over on a new character... It's not worth it. 

The game has quite a lot of content, albeit less than Borderlands 2, and while it definitely feels like you're playing Borderlands 2 in a new map with some new gimmicks for the most part, it's not quite as good. I've seen people complain about drop rates, but that's just a Borderlands standard - you're pretty much going to have times where you'll have absolutely nothing at your level and are having problems as a result. It's a mainstay of the game and it kinda drives you to actually look around a bit more, take more time to notice things and to find the places where you can actually get loot. But I digress. There's plenty of sidequests, though a lot of them are admittedly 'go here, talk to this guy, go here' kinds of things, with not a lot of them being particularly memorable or giving out very good items. Borderlands 2 was better about it because there were plenty of unique guns you could get exclusively from quests that were really good (fibber for anarchy gaige anybody?) but TPS doesn't do as much of that. I'll say that there's a bit better balancing in this than in BL2, namely in the previously mentioned Gaige build being able to destroy pretty much everything with zero effort. But naturally some characters are stronger in different ways than others. An example, your best tank is a girl who's pretty much immune to damage 75% of the time. And she absolutely destroys things at the same time that she's taking all this damage. 

Back to the aforementioned endgame, though, because this is what made this game so bad for most of its playerbase. There are only three raid bosses. If you don't count the seasonal raid boss that replaces one of them. Two of them are completely unimaginative in that they're literally EXACT COPIES of the final boss - not even reskinned, literally exact copies - but buffed up with more health, damage, and stronger minions. And even buffed they don't compare to the all-encompassing power of Terramorphous prior to the UVH releases, and how good he was for making friends at the time since the means of cheesing him wasn't discovered yet and he was impressive, both in difficulty and in size. Terramorphous was one of the first bosses in the game that would smack you in the face and tell you to bring friends. There is nothing like that in TPS. The closest thing is Iwajira, and he's not exactly hard even without cheesing him. Which yes there is a place you can go that works much like Terramorphous', but you have to work a bit harder to get to it. But even that guy doesn't compare to the raid bosses in Borderlands 2. 

With the lore-required removal of Slag as a combat element, given that it predates Borderlands 2, they had to dial things back significantly in the difficulty department because you couldn't abuse the damage buff of slag. So TVH and UVH ended up being 'replay the game with a few new enemies and others buffed, but it's basically no more difficult.' Kinda like old school Diablo 2 and 3. Drops are better, experience is better, but otherwise the game doesn't change much. Which is unfortunate because with the introduction of Cryo damage and how it works, it's very possible to freeze-lock about 90% of the game's enemies with no effort. With the right character, you can do this starting at level 3. There's enemies that can't be frozen or resist cryo, and bosses by and large can't be either, with a few exceptions. But most of the enemies are bandits who like to jump around. And what does an ice cube do when it hits the ground usually? That's right, it shatters. Flying enemies that can be frozen are cake. Bandits that jump around are cake. Bandits that you can see are cake. Cryo makes almost everything far too easy. Especially if you're interested in running a melee build, though admittedly I haven't found any quite as ridiculous as Zero's.

My guess is that the developers hoped for the player to continue playing the game even more after finishing it, just so the player could get to play the game with actually good weapons for a change. 

As some others complains about, the gravity and oxygen concept could be a lot better, yet it didn't bother me that much.

Personally, I'd say that the humor in this game is not really the same as in the previous games, it's sort of more the type that's not supposed to insult someone and is at most times just dull. 

There might be some issue with playing trough the campaign as single-player due to the level balance. I did not do that many side-quests because I thought they were mostly just a waste of time, so I tried sticking mostly to the main quest and finishing the game. At level 20, I suddenly encountered level 24+ enemies and the quest had impossible difficulty. This was not that big of a deal really, because I probably just used about 30 minutes or so to level up so I could continue. Yet, be aware that some grinding to level up might be needed. 



Now the positive things:

The scenery and visual stuff are really nice, lots of cool stuff to look at and neat effects. 

The story of the game is interesting with some twist, turns and lore.

There's some interesting NPC characters in the game and if I remember correctly, there's six characters to choose from as a main character.

There's some new combat features, vehicles, grenades and other things that gives the game something more to do rather than just aim and fire. 

If you like bosses, then there's a lot of them in this game, even a lot of boss-battles that come 
right after another one.

The audio is really good in this game, I use a 7.1 surround headset, and this being able to determine where stuff is from sound is quite the relief in this game compared to a lot of first person shooters. 


The game is not as good as the previous ones and at some times I just wanted to finish it just so I could uninstall it. But if the developers would have gotten their priorities straight rather than prolonging the play-trough time and appealing to players that are fragile, then the whole ordeal could have been so much better even if it was just a seven hour play-trough.

Played the single-player campaign on ubuntu linux 19.04 with radeon mesa graphic drivers. It is a very laid back RPG-esqe game, with lots of weapon upgrades, skill upgrades, and story quests. Move from point to point picking up items and upgrading your character. Some of the quest destinations were not totally obvious, and there was some jumping (especially with vehicles) that was problematic, but overall the storylines were interesting - occasionally funny - with some nice monsters to kill along the way.

Technically, I had no issues playing the game with keyboard and mouse controls. I think it probably used a controller too, The game ran at a high FPS, and I never felt like it was jittery. The graphics were solid, the sound effects were excellent, and the voice acting is excellent. There was no music soundtrack.

I bought this game at a big discount, and I am not sure that I would recommend it for full price, unless you are planning to play it co-operatively. I suspect it would be a lot of fun with a friend or two. Ultimately, the gameplay is a little slow in the single-player mode, with a lot of pick-up and deliver quests. Regardless, I found this to be an enjoyable way to pass some time, especially with the Australian humor to keep me interested.
